question.prompt:
In the plane figure shown below, \(3\) of the unit squares have been shaded. What is the least number of additional unit squares that must be shaded so that the resulting figure has two lines of symmetry?

[Figure 1](figures/2020_AMC_12A_Q06_question_fig1.svg)

solutions.explanation:
The boundary of the figure is a nonsquare rectangle, so its only possible lines of symmetry are its horizontal and vertical midlines. To obtain two lines of symmetry, the shading must agree across both of these lines.

Number the four rows from top to bottom and the five columns from left to right. Write \((r,c)\) for the square in row \(r\), column \(c\). Horizontal reflection pairs rows \(1\) and \(4\), and rows \(2\) and \(3\). Vertical reflection pairs columns \(1\) and \(5\), and columns \(2\) and \(4\), while column \(3\) stays fixed.

Starting with the shaded square \((1,2)\), both symmetries require all four squares
\[
\{(1,2),(1,4),(4,2),(4,4)\}
\]
to be shaded.

The shaded square \((3,3)\) requires the two-square group
\[
\{(2,3),(3,3)\}.
\]
The shaded square \((4,5)\) requires all four squares
\[
\{(1,1),(1,5),(4,1),(4,5)\}.
\]
These groups have no squares in common, so every valid completion must contain at least \(4+2+4=10\) shaded squares. Shading exactly these groups also works: each group is preserved by both reflections. Thus the lower bound is attained.

Since three squares are already shaded, the least additional number is
\[
10-3=\boxed{7},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
solutions.title: Complete the reflected groups
